name: HIAS: US advocacy and litigation for refugees
beneficiaries_note: Our build: refugees waiting abroad for US resettlement, by the largest nationalities in the pipeline (the DRC, Afghanistan, Venezuela, Syria, Myanmar, Sudan, Somalia, Guatemala); a judgment.
summary: HIAS spends about $3 million a year (our estimate, inside its US accounts line) on US advocacy, community engagement and litigation, chiefly as a plaintiff in Pacito v. Trump against the January 2025 suspension of refugee admissions, which let more than 80 approved refugees travel in 2025 before the Ninth Circuit reversed most of the injunction in March 2026. We value the pending case as a small chance (2%) of restoring about 10,000 admissions a year for the years a win counts, fiscal 2025 carrying half of the case's cost, and the 2025 admissions as won, each refugee gaining the US level of consumption over decades against the level where they wait, with HIAS credited 15% of the litigation; at HIAS's own next-dollar figure (49%) it comes to about 0.3 years of healthy life per $1,000, because a refugee resettled in the US gains several doublings of consumption for decades. The result is mostly uncertainty (the chance of success, HIAS's share and the years a win counts span over a thousandfold), and it is discounted for missing data.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programme, including overhead
Extra refugees admitted to the US a year if the suspension is overturned
rows.explainer: The ceiling was 125,000 for fiscal 2025 and 7,500 for fiscal 2026 (annual report PDF p. 5). A win in Pacito v. Trump would at most restore processing of refugees already in the pipeline; the President sets the ceiling, which the case doesn't, so extra admissions would stay far below the old ceiling. 10,000 a year (2,000-50,000). Our judgment.

rows.label: Chance the suspension is overturned by the litigation and advocacy HIAS joins
rows.explainer: On 5 March 2026 the Ninth Circuit held that the President may likely suspend refugee admissions entirely and reversed the injunction on processing and admissions, upholding only the funding of services for refugees already in the US (IRAP, https://refugeerights.org/news-resources/ninth-circuit-rules-government-must-fund-domestic-refugee-resettlement-services-reverses-order-requiring-continued-refugee-processing). What remains is a rehearing, the Supreme Court or a new suit, against an administration that has won most immigration stays. One event, drawn as happens or doesn't. 2% (0.5-6%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Years a win counts
rows.explainer: The site's one number of years a won reform brings a change forward (docs/normalization.md 2.9): a later administration might restore admissions anyway.

rows.label: Years until a win takes effect
rows.explainer: Further appeals after the March 2026 ruling and rebuilding the overseas processing pipeline: 2 years (1-3). Our judgment.

rows.label: Fiscal 2025's share of the resources the case will take
rows.explainer: The case began in February 2025 and goes on; fiscal 2025 carried the filing, the injunction hearings and the appeal, about half of what it will take (a third if it runs three years like it, all of it if it ends now). 50% (33-100%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Refugees' consumption where they wait, as a share of the host country's average
rows.explainer: Refugees referred for resettlement wait in camps and cities in East Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America, mostly below their hosts. 60% (40-90%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Refugees' consumption while waiting (PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: Refugees in the US pipeline wait mainly in East Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania), the Middle East (Jordan, Türkiye, Egypt), Latin America (Colombia, Ecuador) and South Asia (Pakistan, Malaysia); the site's survey figures for Kenya, Egypt, Peru and Bangladesh stand in for them equally (a judgment).

rows.label: Years a resettled refugee gains in the US
rows.explainer: Refugees admitted are of every age, many children; without resettlement most would stay displaced for decades (protracted situations average over 20 years). 30 years (15-45). Our judgment.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per refugee admitted, discounted over their years
rows.explainer: Each year's cohort of extra refugees gains the US level against the level where they wait, every year they stay, on the site's log-income scale.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained per refugee (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Zero: the gain is counted as income and mortality; safety and family reunion are an unmodelled share (ue_family_share), so they aren't counted twice.

rows.label: Illness averted per refugee admitted, in healthy years
rows.explainer: Better treatment of chronic and infectious illness in the US than in camps and poor cities, over the years in the US: 0.02 healthy years per refugee (0-0.1), apart from the income and the mortality rows. Our judgment.

rows.label: Excess yearly mortality where refugees wait, over the US (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Crude death rates in long-running camps sit near or above their hosts' (Kenya and Uganda about 0.5-0.6% a year for young populations, UN WPP) against far lower age-specific rates in the US for the same young people. 0.2 points a year (0-0.5). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: Children are about 40% of refugees (UNHCR) and young children die at higher rates in camps, while adults far outnumber them over decades in the US. 30% (10-45%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Deaths averted per refugee admitted, discounted over their years
Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for children under five and adults 15-49, times your value of a life.

source.quote: More than 80 refugees who would have otherwise been stuck in limbo have since successfully resettled and reunited with their families thanks to injunctions secured through our lawsuit.

rows.explainer: The same count as charityevals' model of IRAP's litigation, which shares the credit; HIAS's annual report calls it 'a small number of vulnerable refugees in the summer of 2025' (PDF p. 8), and IRAP's 5 March 2026 page says more than a hundred by then (https://refugeerights.org/news-resources/ninth-circuit-rules-government-must-fund-domestic-refugee-resettlement-services-reverses-order-requiring-continued-refugee-processing), some after HIAS's fiscal year.

rows.explainer: The value of resettlement is the consumption gap and the extra years, judged from survey figures rather than measured for these refugees. 0.7 (0.5-0.9). Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: the pending win counts 1 here, since whether it would come anyway is the question the years counted answer (Convention 5); the injunction's admissions carry pac_counterfactual_adj, applied in refugees_counted.

rows.label: HIAS's share of the resources behind the litigation and advocacy
rows.explainer: By resources: the International Refugee Assistance Project and pro bono co-counsel carry most of the litigation's work (a judged three-fifths); HIAS, Church World Service and Lutheran Community Services Northwest, the organisational plaintiffs (annual report PDF p. 8), share the rest with the individual refugees, about an eighth each; HIAS's own advocacy and congregations add a little to its share against the other agencies' and coalitions' campaigns. 15% (5-30%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Share of a win enforced (pending win only)
rows.explainer: Court orders on admissions have been slow-walked and narrowed; a restored programme takes years to rebuild its overseas pipeline. 70% (40-90%). Our judgment. Applied to the pending win only: the 2025 admissions are counted as they happened.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): the chance of success, the admissions a win restores and HIAS's share are judgments.

Unmodelled: Global Health Council v. Trump
rows.explainer: HIAS is one of many plaintiffs in the case that forced payment of frozen foreign-aid awards for work already done (annual report PDF p. 8): a tiny share of a large sum. +5% (0 to +15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: funding for refugees already in the US
rows.explainer: The Ninth Circuit upheld the order that the government fund resettlement services for refugees already admitted: case management and cash for people who arrived before the suspension. +3% (0 to +10%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: safety and family reunion of the refugees admitted
rows.explainer: Beyond consumption and mortality: safety from persecution and families reunited (many refugees join relatives already here). +3% (0 to +8%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: community mobilisation and support for refugees
rows.explainer: 20,400 people contacted their representatives 41,600 times, 284 congregations held Refugee Shabbat and vigils ran in 14 states (annual report PDF p. 7): goodwill toward refugees beyond the litigation. +5% (0 to +15%). Our judgment.

rows.label: Unmodelled: backlash
rows.explainer: Litigation and protest can harden opposition. -1% (-5% to 0). Our judgment.
